title: Trentino-Alto Adige's Metano Premium Is Shrinking — Even as GPL Pulls Further Ahead of the Rest of Italy
dek: A week-by-week look at how the region's four fuel prices are diverging from the national average as autumn sets in.
executive_summary: On September 16, drivers in Trentino-Alto Adige paid €2.1872/L for self-service Benzina (up €0.0132, +0.61% day-over-day) and €2.3068/L for Gasolio (up €0.0140, +0.61%), against national self-service averages of €2.1435 and €2.2728 respectively — the region running about 2.0% above the national Benzina price and 1.5% above Gasolio. GPL held nearly flat at €0.8024/kg (+0.25% on the day) and Metano didn't move at all from the day before, staying at €1.9660/kg, but both trade well above the national floor: GPL 6.2% above the national average and Metano fully 11.7% above it. Of the region's 392 registered stations, 372 reported prices today (94.9%), comfortably ahead of the 90.2% national reporting rate.

Zooming out to the nine weeks of data tracked since the week of July 20, the more interesting story is how each fuel's regional premium over the national average is moving, not just how big it is today. Metano's regional premium — long the region's most extreme outlier — has actually narrowed by about 27%, from a near-30-cent gap in late July to roughly 22 cents now, because the national Metano price has climbed faster (+16.5%) than Trentino-Alto Adige's own Metano price (+9.3%). GPL is moving the opposite way: its regional premium has widened by roughly 49% over the same stretch, as the region's GPL price crept up 1.4% while the national average essentially stood still (-0.6%). Benzina and Gasolio, meanwhile, have tracked the national trend almost lockstep — both up roughly 4-8% regionally and nationally with no meaningful shift in the premium either way.

fuel_sections.heading: Benzina: Tracking the National Curve, Not Breaking From It
paragraphs: Self-service Benzina in Trentino-Alto Adige closed September 16 at €2.1872/L, up €0.0132 (+0.61%) from the previous day — a move roughly in line with the steady national climb this month. That puts the region 2.0% above the €2.1435 national self-service average, a premium that has held remarkably steady since midsummer.

Across the nine tracked weeks — from the week of July 20 (€2.0210) to the week of September 14 (€2.1747) — regional Benzina is up 7.61%. Nationally, the same period saw self-service Benzina rise from €1.9756 to €2.1309, a 7.86% increase, very slightly ahead of the region. The regional premium over the national average has therefore barely budged, from about 4.5 cents in late July to about 4.4 cents now: Trentino-Alto Adige's Benzina prices aren't diverging from the rest of Italy, they're rising in step with it.

fuel_sections.heading: Gasolio Keeps Pace With the Nationwide Climb Too
paragraphs: Gasolio (self-service) in the region reached €2.3068/L on September 16, up €0.0140 (+0.61%) day-over-day — matching Benzina's daily move almost to the decimal. That's 1.5% above the €2.2728 national self-service average, one of the smaller regional premiums among the four fuels tracked here.

Over the nine-week window from the week of July 20 (€2.2063) to the week of September 14 (€2.2927), regional Gasolio rose 3.92%, essentially matching the national move from €2.1747 to €2.2585 (+3.85%). The premium gap has widened only marginally, from about 3.2 cents to about 3.4 cents — Gasolio, like Benzina, is a fuel where Trentino-Alto Adige is simply riding the same wave as the rest of the country, not setting its own course.

fuel_sections.heading: GPL: The Region's Premium Over Italy Is Quietly Widening
paragraphs: GPL held at €0.8024/kg on September 16, up just €0.0020 (+0.25%) on the day — the smallest daily move of the four fuels. But it carries the second-largest regional premium of the group: 6.2% above the €0.7554 national self-service average.

The multi-week trend is what makes GPL notable. From the week of July 20 (€0.7912) to the week of September 14 (€0.8024), the regional price rose 1.42%, while the national average actually fell slightly, from €0.7592 to €0.7547 (-0.59%). That divergence means the region's GPL premium over the national average has widened by roughly 49% in under two months — from about a 3.2-cent gap to about a 4.8-cent gap. Of the four fuels tracked, GPL is the one where Trentino-Alto Adige is most visibly pulling away from the national trend.

fuel_sections.heading: Metano's Enormous Regional Premium Is Actually Shrinking
paragraphs: Metano was flat at €1.9660/kg on September 16 — no change from the prior day — but it carries by far the largest regional premium of any fuel: 11.7% above the €1.7608 national self-service average, a gap of just over 20 cents.

That's still a striking gap, but the more interesting trend is the direction it's moving. From the week of July 20 (€1.7993) to the week of September 14 (€1.9660), regional Metano rose 9.26%. Nationally, though, Metano climbed much faster — from €1.4999 to €1.7477, a 16.51% jump, nearly double the regional rate of increase. The result: the region's Metano premium over the national average has actually narrowed by about 27%, from a near-30-cent gap in late July to roughly 22 cents now. Trentino-Alto Adige still pays a steep premium for Metano, but the rest of Italy is closing the gap faster than the region is pulling away.

network_section.heading: A Reporting Rate Well Above the National Average
paragraphs: Trentino-Alto Adige has 392 registered fuel stations, of which 372 reported prices on September 16 — a 94.9% reporting rate. That's noticeably higher than the 90.2% rate seen across Italy's roughly 24,000 registered stations (21,645 reporting nationally today).

A high reporting rate matters because it's what makes the region's average prices trustworthy day to day: with only a handful of stations not reporting, Trentino-Alto Adige's figures reflect close to the full local market rather than a thin, potentially unrepresentative sample. It's also a useful sanity check on the numbers in this report — a sudden drop in the reporting rate would be the first sign that a day's regional average should be read with more caution.

methodology_section.heading: How This Report Gets Made — Without a Spreadsheet in Sight
paragraphs: Everything in this report — the daily price data, the region-of-the-day rotation, the week-by-week trend analysis, and the prose itself — is produced automatically, every day, by an unattended pipeline built with Claude Code. A scheduled job pulls the day's price and station-registry data, deterministically picks a region to feature (a fixed alphabetical rotation over Italy's 20 regions, keyed to the calendar date), computes the weekly regional-vs-national comparisons, and then an AI agent reads those real numbers and writes the analysis from scratch — nothing here is a template with numbers dropped in.

Contrast that with the traditional way this kind of tracking gets done: someone manually downloading a CSV each morning, pasting it into a spreadsheet, recalculating a handful of averages by hand, and writing up a summary if and when they get around to it. That approach doesn't scale past one or two fuels or one region, and it breaks the moment someone forgets a day. This pipeline runs the same way every single day, covers all four fuels and all 20 regions in rotation, and produces a full report plus a live dashboard update without anyone opening Excel.

caption:
Today's Fuel Dashboard spotlight: Trentino-Alto Adige, where diesel and petrol are simply riding the same nationwide wave — but LPG and natural gas are telling two opposite stories. The region's Metano premium over the rest of Italy has narrowed by about 27% since July, even though it still costs roughly 20 cents more per kg there than the national average. GPL is doing the reverse: its regional premium has widened by nearly 49% in under two months.

Fuel Dashboard is a fully automated, self-updating site tracking Italian fuel prices across all 20 regions, every province, and thousands of stations and comuni — rebuilt and republished every single day. No one opens a spreadsheet to make this happen: an unattended pipeline built with Claude Code pulls the data, picks the day's featured region, runs the trend analysis, writes the report, and redeploys the live dashboard, start to finish.

That's the case for building this kind of thing with AI tools instead of maintaining it by hand: a one-person side project can now ship daily, data-grounded analysis at a depth and consistency that would take a small team to maintain manually — and it never misses a day.
